flashcards.q: What does a passing golden-master/snapshot test actually prove?
flashcards.a: Only that the current output is unchanged from a previously captured baseline -- it never proves the baseline was correct. A snapshot captured from buggy behavior enshrines the bug forever.

flashcards.q: What percentage of Google's tests exhibit some flakiness, and what fraction of pass-to-fail transitions there are flaky rather than real bugs?
flashcards.a: About 16% of tests show some flakiness; roughly 84% of pass-to-fail transitions at Google are flaky, not real regressions.

flashcards.q: What is Microsoft's flaky-test quarantine policy, and what result did it produce?
flashcards.a: A flaky test is removed from the blocking gate; if not fixed within two weeks it is deleted outright. This hard SLA prevented the quarantine list from growing indefinitely and produced an 18% reduction in overall flakiness within six months.

flashcards.q: What is the mechanical difference between a flaky test and a test that's genuinely intermittently failing due to a real bug?
flashcards.a: Flakiness is variance in result on the SAME commit across repeated runs -- nothing changed but the outcome did. A test failing on some commits and passing on others isn't flaky; it may be correctly detecting a real intermittent bug in the system under test.

flashcards.q: Name four concrete root causes of test flakiness.
flashcards.a: Unmocked wall-clock time/timezone assertions; fixed sleep() instead of wait-for-condition on async operations; shared mutable state racing across parallel test workers; test order dependence (test B only passes if test A ran first).

flashcards.q: Why is reflexively running --updateSnapshot on every CI failure dangerous?
flashcards.a: It converts every mismatch into an automatic, unreviewed re-baseline -- if the mismatch was caused by a real bug, the bug becomes the new golden master and the suite certifies it going forward.

flashcards.q: When should tolerance-based regression assertions replace exact-diff golden-file snapshots?
flashcards.a: Whenever output has legitimate run-to-run variance that isn't a regression -- floating-point metrics from retrained models, timestamps, generated IDs -- since literal diffing there produces constant false failures teams learn to ignore.

flashcards.q: What did Slack's flake detection rollout change, in numbers?
flashcards.a: Main branch pass rate went from roughly 20% (before automated flake detection/suppression) to under 4% false failures afterward.

flashcards.q: What is Michael Feathers' golden-master technique used for, and from which book?
flashcards.a: From 'Working Effectively with Legacy Code' (2004): capture current (not necessarily correct) output as a baseline before refactoring undocumented legacy code, since 'didn't change unintentionally' is the only safety net available until correctness can be verified independently.

flashcards.q: What is the core snapshot-testing discipline that prevents it from becoming noise?
flashcards.a: Keep snapshots small and focused on one concern, and review every snapshot diff in code review with the same scrutiny as an implementation diff -- large, frequently-changing snapshots get rubber-stamped rather than read.
